questions.questionText: What is one important difference between a conventional fixed-flow program and an AI agent?
questions.hint: Consider who decides what to do next.

options.text: An agent can use a model to make some decisions about what to do next
A fixed-flow program always learns new behavior from every request
An agent cannot follow predefined rules
A fixed-flow program always has access to external tools

summary: An agent uses a model to make some decisions as it works toward a goal.
A fixed-flow program follows steps explicitly laid out in its code.

questions.questionText: What can an agent do after deciding a tool would help?
questions.hint: Think about what happens after the tool returns its result.

options.text: Choose the tool, provide inputs, inspect the result, and decide what to do next
Assume the tool succeeded without checking its result
Show the user the tool's source code instead of calling it
Stop processing the request immediately

summary: An agent can select and call a tool, inspect its result, and continue or respond.
The tool result becomes part of the agent's decision process.

questions.questionText: What does the ReAct idea describe?
questions.hint: The name combines thinking with doing.

options.text: Reasoning interleaved with actions
A format for storing API keys
A method for converting text into embeddings
A transport used only by local MCP servers

summary: ReAct is a reasoning-and-action pattern used to explain agent tool-use loops.
It is background for understanding agents that reason, act, and consider results.

questions.questionText: Does every request to an agent need a tool call?
questions.hint: Some requests can be answered without external information or actions.

options.text: No. An agent may answer directly when a tool is unnecessary
Yes. Every agent response must call every available tool
Yes. Tools are required for all language generation
No. Agents are not allowed to use tools

summary: An agent can answer directly or use a tool depending on the request.
Tool use should be selected when it helps, not treated as mandatory.

questions.questionText: In a coding-agent workflow, what is a sensible sequence before the final response?
questions.hint: The agent needs to observe what its chosen actions did.

options.text: Inspect information, select tools, observe results, and respond when the task is complete
Call tools at random and ignore their outputs
Respond first, then decide what the user asked
Ask the model to execute code without application controls

summary: Tool use involves observing, acting, and considering outcomes before responding.
The agent can repeat the loop if the task needs more than one action.

questions.questionText: Why might an agent need a tool rather than relying only on its model?
questions.hint: Think about access to current or external information.

options.text: A tool can access external data or perform actions such as reading files or querying an API
A tool guarantees that every answer is correct
A tool permanently changes the model's training
A tool removes the need to validate inputs

summary: Tools extend an agent with access to information or actions beyond a model-only response.
Examples include current data, files, APIs, and databases.

questions.questionText: What problem does MCP address when agents need to use external tools?
questions.hint: Consider what happens if every agent implements the same integration separately.

options.text: It provides a common way to connect clients to separately implemented tools
It replaces all APIs with one database
It prevents clients from using external services
It requires every tool to be part of the model

summary: MCP offers a common protocol so tools can be reused by compatible clients.
This avoids implementing every tool separately inside each agent.

questions.questionText: What role does MCP play in an AI application's tool architecture?
questions.hint: It connects the application side to the side providing tools.

options.text: A protocol connecting MCP clients to tools exposed by MCP servers
A programming language used to train LLMs
A database for storing API credentials
A user interface for creating documents

summary: MCP defines a common way for clients and servers to communicate about available tools.
Clients can use tools provided separately by servers.

questions.questionText: What is an MCP client?
questions.hint: It is the application that connects to the server.

options.text: An application or agent that communicates with MCP servers
A function that can only run in a browser
A server that publishes API documentation
A database record returned by a tool

summary: An MCP client implements the client side of the protocol and communicates with servers.
The client may be an AI-enabled application or agent.

questions.questionText: What is an MCP server?
questions.hint: It makes callable operations available to clients.

options.text: A service that makes one or more tools available to clients
The language model's hidden reasoning process
A user account used to sign in to a website
A JSON file containing only quiz questions

summary: An MCP server exposes tools to compatible clients.
The server can be implemented separately from the client application.

questions.questionText: What is an MCP tool in the basic model?
questions.hint: It is something callable with defined inputs and an outcome.

options.text: A callable operation, commonly a function with inputs and a result
A model's training dataset
A network cable between two computers
A user interface theme

summary: A tool performs a defined operation when called with suitable inputs.
MCP servers make tools available to clients.

questions.questionText: Which are examples of applications that could be MCP clients?
questions.hint: A client is an application that connects to MCP servers.

options.text: A coding assistant
A personal assistant
A voice-oriented assistant
A protocol message identifier

summary: Coding assistants, personal assistants, and voice assistants can all be clients.
A message identifier is protocol data, not an application.

questions.questionText: What tool information is presented to a model, and what is not?
questions.hint: The model needs enough metadata to choose and call a tool.

options.text: The tool name, description, and input schema may be presented; implementation code is not
Only the implementation code is presented
The model is always given unrestricted access to the server's files
No information about tools is presented

summary: Tool metadata helps a model understand and call a tool without exposing its implementation code.
This distinction also means descriptions alone cannot prove what the code does.

questions.questionText: Why can MCP servers make agent systems more modular?
questions.hint: Consider whether tools have to be built into one specific agent.

options.text: Tools can be implemented separately and shared across compatible clients
Every server must contain a complete AI model
Clients can no longer use more than one tool
All server code is copied into each model

summary: Separate servers can provide reusable capabilities to compatible clients.
This supports modularity and avoids duplicating integrations in each agent.

questions.questionText: Why consult MCP SDK and protocol documentation when building a server?
questions.hint: Documentation describes how the SDK and protocol should be used.

options.text: It provides implementation guidance for the protocol and SDK
It automatically writes and secures every tool
It removes the need to test the server
It provides user passwords for remote services

summary: Protocol and SDK documentation helps developers implement a compatible server.
Relevant documentation can also help a coding assistant generate code that follows the intended APIs.

questions.questionText: What is FastMCP used for when building an MCP server in Python?
questions.hint: It is a Python interface for creating MCP servers.

options.text: A higher-level Python interface for creating servers and exposing functions as tools
A cloud provider's OAuth password manager
A vector database query language
A replacement for all HTTP methods

summary: FastMCP is a higher-level Python interface for creating MCP servers and registering functions as tools.
It helps reduce the setup needed to expose functions as tools.

questions.questionText: Why should an MCP tool have a clear name and description?
questions.hint: The client or model uses this information when deciding what to call.

options.text: They help clients and models understand the tool's purpose and when to use it
They hide the tool from every client
They guarantee the tool implementation is safe
They replace the tool's input validation

summary: Names and descriptions help explain the tool's purpose.
They do not replace testing, validation, or security review of its implementation.

questions.questionText: What purpose do parameter types and input schemas serve?
questions.hint: They describe what information a tool expects.

options.text: They describe acceptable tool inputs so clients can provide suitable values
They encrypt every response from the server
They decide which hosting provider to use
They store the model's conversation history permanently

summary: Types and schemas describe the inputs a tool accepts.
Clients can use that information to construct suitable calls.

questions.questionText: What is the MCP Inspector for?
questions.hint: It lets you examine and invoke tools without relying on an agent to choose them.

options.text: Inspecting available tools and testing calls against a server
Creating OAuth identities for every user
Automatically deploying a server to the cloud
Replacing the MCP client in production

summary: The Inspector helps developers connect to a server, list its tools, and invoke them.
This isolates tool testing from an agent's tool-selection behavior.

questions.questionText: Why might an MCP server fail to start if its configuration is incomplete?
questions.hint: The server may depend on configuration such as an API credential.

options.text: A required setting or environment variable may be missing
The tool description has too many words
The server always needs a graphical user interface
A JSON-RPC identifier is missing from every startup command

summary: Servers may require environment variables or settings such as API keys.
Configuration should be supplied securely and checked when the server starts.

questions.questionText: Why use environment variables for API keys instead of hard-coding them?
questions.hint: Think about what happens if source code is shared publicly.

options.text: To reduce the chance of exposing secrets in source code or a public repository
To make the API key visible to the language model
To ensure the key never expires
To disable authentication on the API

summary: Keeping secrets outside source code reduces accidental exposure.
Environment variables are one configuration mechanism; they still need appropriate protection.

questions.questionText: What role can uv play in a Python MCP project?
questions.hint: It helps manage a Python project's setup.

options.text: Managing project setup, environments, and dependencies
Serving as an OAuth authorization server
Creating embeddings for every language model
Translating HTTP into JSON-RPC

summary: uv can manage Python project setup, environments, and dependencies.
It helps prepare the development environment for an MCP server.

questions.questionText: What does API stand for, and what does it provide?
questions.hint: It is an interface intended for software-to-software interaction.

options.text: Application Programming Interface; a programmatic way to access a service or its data
Automated Protocol Identifier; a language model training method
Application Permission Index; a type of database
Agent Processing Instruction; a graphical interface

summary: An API is an Application Programming Interface.
It lets software interact programmatically with another service.

questions.questionText: How does an API differ from a graphical user interface?
questions.hint: One is typically used by people directly; the other by software.

options.text: A graphical interface is for direct human use; an API enables programmatic requests
An API can only be used by people with a mouse
A graphical interface is always more secure than an API
An API is a visual layout of buttons and menus

summary: A graphical interface helps people interact directly with an application.
An API exposes operations for software to call.

questions.questionText: What is an API endpoint?
questions.hint: It is a specific route or URL used to request an operation.

options.text: A specific URL or route for requesting an API operation or data
The final answer generated by an LLM
The private source code of an API client
A user permission scope

summary: An endpoint identifies a particular API route or operation.
Clients send requests to endpoints and process the responses.

questions.questionText: What are a request and a response in a typical API interaction?
questions.hint: The client sends one, and the service returns the other.

options.text: The client sends a request; the service processes it and returns a response
The service sends a request to itself and hides the response
A request is an API key and a response is a password
They are two names for an endpoint

summary: A client sends a request to an API, which returns a response.
The response often contains requested data or the result of an operation.

questions.questionText: What is the GET HTTP method commonly used for?
questions.hint: It is used when the client wants to retrieve data.

options.text: Retrieving data
Deleting the API server
Encrypting an API key
Creating a new MCP transport

summary: GET is commonly used to retrieve data from an API.
For example, a client might use GET to fetch a list of news headlines.

questions.questionText: What is the POST HTTP method commonly used for?
questions.hint: It commonly sends data to a server.

options.text: Sending data to a server or creating a resource
Retrieving only public documentation
Opening a local stdio connection
Validating a JWT signature without a server

summary: POST is commonly used to send data to a server or create a resource.
It does not itself encrypt data or guarantee that request data is never logged.

questions.questionText: Which set contains HTTP methods commonly used for updating or deleting resources?
questions.hint: They are often used for updating or deleting resources.

options.text: PUT, PATCH, and DELETE
STDIO, SSE, and JSON
OAuth, JWT, and scope
GET, MCP, and FastMCP

summary: PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are additional HTTP methods.
Which method to use depends on the API's design and documentation.

questions.questionText: Why might an API require an API key?
questions.hint: The service may need to identify or authorize the caller.

options.text: To identify or authorize the caller before providing access
To convert every request into an MCP tool
To guarantee that the service is always available
To make the endpoint easier to guess

summary: An API key may be required to identify or authorize a caller.
Keys should be treated as secrets and protected.

questions.questionText: What can an API client such as Bruno help a learner do?
questions.hint: It allows requests to be sent and their responses inspected.

options.text: Send API requests, adjust methods or parameters, and inspect responses
Automatically make every API public
Replace the server's authentication policy
Create model embeddings without text

summary: API clients help learners explore endpoints and understand request and response behavior.
They are useful for testing an API before wrapping it in an MCP tool.

questions.questionText: What does JSON-RPC describe in MCP communication?
questions.hint: It describes message structure, not the physical communication channel.

options.text: The structure of request and response messages exchanged by client and server
The programming language used to implement every server
The cloud host that runs a remote server
The permission granted by an OAuth scope

summary: JSON-RPC describes the shape of requests and responses.
It is distinct from the transport carrying those messages.

questions.questionText: Which items are commonly included in a JSON-RPC tool-call request?
questions.hint: A request needs to identify what to call, with which inputs, and correlate the response.

options.text: The method to call
The method parameters
A request identifier
The server's source-code repository password

summary: The request identifies a method, its parameters, and a request ID.
The ID helps correlate the response with the request.

questions.questionText: How does a successful tool result return to the client?
questions.hint: The server returns a response after executing the requested operation.

options.text: The server sends a JSON-RPC response containing the result
The model reads the server's source code directly
The client assumes success without receiving a message
The result is returned only by a graphical interface

summary: After executing a tool, the server returns a response containing its result.
The client can then provide that result to the agent's decision process.

questions.questionText: What does “transport” mean in MCP?
questions.hint: It is the channel used to carry protocol messages.

options.text: The communication channel carrying messages between client and server
The schema defining each tool's arguments
The tool's implementation language
A list of OAuth scopes

summary: A transport carries MCP messages between the communicating parties.
It is distinct from the format of the messages themselves.

questions.questionText: What is stdio transport commonly used for?
questions.hint: The client and server usually run on the same computer.

options.text: Local communication with a server process using standard input and output
Communication with any cloud server through a public website
Storing vectors in a database
Exchanging OAuth scopes without a client

summary: Stdio is commonly used when a local client starts or communicates with a server process.
The communication uses standard input and output.

questions.questionText: What is Streamable HTTP used for?
questions.hint: It is appropriate for a server exposed through an HTTP URL.

options.text: Communicating with an MCP server exposed over HTTP, including a remote server
Calling a Python function without any client-server message
Managing Python package versions
Replacing tool input schemas

summary: Streamable HTTP carries MCP communication over HTTP.
It supports connecting to HTTP-accessible servers, including remote deployments.

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes Server-Sent Events (SSE) in relation to MCP transports?
questions.hint: Consider how SSE relates historically to Streamable HTTP and check the protocol version supported by an implementation.

options.text: SSE is an earlier HTTP transport; implementations should follow the MCP protocol version and SDK they support
It describes SSE as a tool input schema
It says SSE is an API authentication token
It describes SSE as the Python package manager

summary: SSE was used as an earlier MCP HTTP transport, while Streamable HTTP is the newer transport described in current MCP guidance.
Transport support can depend on protocol and SDK versions, so check the documentation for the implementation you use.

questions.questionText: Why can a tool's description alone not establish that it is safe?
questions.hint: The model typically does not inspect the implementation code.

options.text: The code could behave differently from what its description claims
Descriptions always contain executable code
MCP servers cannot have descriptions
A description guarantees the server has no permissions

summary: The model sees metadata, not necessarily the server implementation.
A misleading description is not a substitute for reviewing and trusting the code.

questions.questionText: What is a key risk of running an untrusted stdio server locally?
questions.hint: The server code executes on your computer.

options.text: It may access files, environment values, or network resources available to its process
It can only display its tool description
It cannot execute code because stdio is a transport
It automatically runs in a remote sandbox

summary: A local server executes code on the user's computer with the process's available resources.
Use trusted servers and consider what access they receive.

questions.questionText: What precautions are sensible before installing a community MCP server?
questions.hint: Consider the publisher, source code, and whether the server is trustworthy.

options.text: Check who published it
Prefer trusted or official sources
Inspect its source when possible
Assume popularity guarantees safety

summary: Checking the publisher, source, and trusted distribution can reduce risk.
Popularity or a listing alone does not prove that code is safe.

questions.questionText: Why specify or pin a server version when installing one?
questions.hint: Version selection helps control which code is installed.

options.text: To control the version and avoid unintentionally installing unverified code
To let the server ignore all permission checks
To make the server run without a transport
To guarantee there will never be a security vulnerability

summary: Pinning a version makes the selected code version explicit.
It helps with reproducibility but does not guarantee that the version is secure.

questions.questionText: Does using a remote server eliminate security and privacy concerns?
questions.hint: The code runs elsewhere, but data and provider trust still matter.

options.text: No. The provider must be trusted and data sent to the server still needs protection
Yes. Remote servers cannot access user data
Yes. Hosting automatically encrypts every kind of data
No. Remote servers always run with administrator access

summary: Remote hosting changes where code runs, not whether the provider is trustworthy.
Consider the information sent to the service and how it is protected.

questions.questionText: Which items should developers avoid committing to a public repository for a RAG application?
questions.hint: Keep secrets and local data out of source control.

options.text: Environment files containing secrets
Local document data
The local Chroma database
A README explaining how to run the project

summary: Secrets and local data or databases should not be committed publicly.
A README with safe setup instructions is not itself a secret.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between a localhost HTTP MCP server and a cloud-hosted remote server?
questions.hint: The key difference is where the server process runs.

options.text: Localhost runs on the developer's computer; a remote server runs on another machine
Localhost always uses stdio, while remote servers cannot use HTTP
A remote server is always safe, while localhost is never safe
They differ only in the tool names

summary: A localhost server runs on the local computer; a cloud-hosted server runs elsewhere.
Both can expose HTTP endpoints, but deployment and trust considerations differ.

questions.questionText: Why might a developer integrate an MCP server into a FastAPI application?
questions.hint: A web application can host MCP endpoints alongside other backend capabilities.

options.text: To provide a broader backend for MCP and related services such as authentication or other endpoints
To prevent the server from receiving HTTP requests
To make all tools run in the model's training process
To replace every API with stdio

summary: FastAPI can host MCP endpoints as part of a broader backend application.
Related services can include authentication and other HTTP routes.

questions.questionText: When can hosting multiple MCP servers in one application be useful?
questions.hint: Consider whether the servers are related and benefit from sharing a host.

options.text: When they are related or benefit from being hosted together
Whenever servers have unrelated security requirements
Only when they use different programming languages
It is required by MCP for every deployment

summary: Related servers may be hosted together when it is useful.
Unrelated servers may be better separated.

questions.questionText: Which sequence is a sensible general process for deploying a remote MCP server?
questions.hint: The deployed URL needs to be tested after the host is configured.

options.text: Prepare the app, configure the host and environment, deploy, then test the URL
Deploy first, add the server code later, and never test
Publish API keys in the repository, then deploy
Remove all configuration before starting the server

summary: Deployment involves preparing the application, configuring the hosting service, and deploying it.
Testing the resulting endpoint helps confirm that the remote server is reachable.

questions.questionText: Why must a client use the correct HTTP URL and path when connecting to a server?
questions.hint: The MCP endpoint may be mounted at a specific route.

options.text: The endpoint may use a specific path, and the wrong route can cause connection errors
The URL determines which tool implementation the model sees
HTTP paths are only used to store embeddings
A client can connect only if the URL contains an API key

summary: Clients must connect to the correct host and MCP endpoint path.
A wrong URL or route can prevent successful communication.

questions.questionText: Which settings are commonly important when deploying a web-based MCP server to a hosting platform?
questions.hint: The server must bind correctly and receive its required configuration.

options.text: Binding the host appropriately
Using the expected port
Setting required environment variables
Committing all secret values to source control

summary: Host binding, the expected port, and required environment variables are common deployment considerations.
Exact settings vary by hosting platform and should be checked in its documentation.

questions.questionText: Why does a remote MCP server need authentication and authorization?
questions.hint: The server may expose sensitive data or actions.

options.text: To control who can connect and what they are permitted to do
To make every tool publicly available
To replace the need for tool input schemas
To ensure responses contain no errors

summary: Authentication and authorization help protect remote tools and data.
They establish who is accessing the server and what access is permitted.

questions.questionText: Why can local API-key configuration be inconvenient for nontechnical users?
questions.hint: Think about what a user may need to edit or obtain.

options.text: They may need to edit configuration files and obtain or enter keys themselves
API keys can only be entered into a vector database
Local configuration prevents all tools from working
It requires users to write the MCP protocol

summary: Manual API-key configuration can require users to find credentials and edit files.
OAuth-style flows can improve the experience in some cases.

questions.questionText: What does OAuth help a user avoid sharing directly with an MCP server?
questions.hint: The server can receive a token rather than the user's underlying credentials.

options.text: The user's underlying credentials for another service
The tool's public description
The MCP transport name
The API endpoint path

summary: OAuth flows can let a service receive a token rather than the user's underlying credentials.
The server should validate the token and its permitted access.

questions.questionText: What is a scope used for in OAuth-based access to a protected MCP server?
questions.hint: It represents a permission that can be granted or required.

options.text: Representing a permission, such as access to a particular tool
Choosing whether the server uses JSON or Python
Storing the server's source code
Selecting an HTTP port automatically

summary: A scope describes a permission associated with a token.
A server can check whether the token grants the permission needed for a tool.

questions.questionText: What can a 401 response communicate in an OAuth-enabled MCP authorization flow?
questions.hint: It signals that the request is unauthorized and can point a client toward authentication metadata.

options.text: It indicates the request is unauthorized and may provide metadata to find the authorization process
It confirms that the tool call succeeded
It means the server has permanently deleted the tool
It encrypts the client configuration

summary: A 401 response indicates that the request is unauthorized.
A server may include metadata that helps a compatible client discover how to authenticate.

questions.questionText: Why might authorization metadata endpoints be accessible without a bearer token?
questions.hint: A client needs some public information before it can authenticate.

options.text: The client needs the metadata to learn how to authenticate
Metadata endpoints execute all protected tools
Bearer tokens are never used by remote servers
The metadata endpoint stores user passwords

summary: A client may need authorization metadata before it can obtain a token.
Leaving that discovery information accessible supports the authentication flow.

questions.questionText: What should a server do when it receives a bearer token?
questions.hint: Checking that a token exists is not the same as checking that it is valid.

options.text: Validate the token and check relevant permissions
Accept any non-empty string as valid
Send the token to the language model for storage
Ignore the token and grant administrator access

summary: A server should validate tokens rather than merely checking for their presence.
Validation can include checking token properties and required permissions.

questions.questionText: When may a tool call require a scope check?
questions.hint: Some tools may require a specific permission.

options.text: When the requested tool has a permission requirement that the server must verify
Only when the client uses stdio
For every public documentation page, regardless of policy
Scopes are never checked after token validation

summary: A server can associate a required scope with a protected tool.
It checks whether the caller's token grants that permission.

questions.questionText: What problem does RAG help address?
questions.hint: It supplies external or private document information as context to a model.

options.text: It lets a model answer using retrieved external or private document information
It guarantees that a model never makes an error
It permanently trains every document into model weights
It replaces the need for a language model

summary: RAG retrieves relevant information and supplies it as context to a language model.
This can help answer questions about external or private material.

questions.questionText: What are the three broad stages of a typical RAG workflow?
questions.hint: Prepare the data, find relevant content, then generate an answer.

options.text: ETL or document preparation, retrieval, and generation
Authentication, authorization, and deployment
Prompting, compiling, and encrypting
Tokenizing, hosting, and deleting

summary: RAG commonly includes document preparation, retrieval, and generation.
The retrieved context is provided to the model to support its response.

questions.questionText: What does ETL mean in the RAG explanation?
questions.hint: The letters refer to preparing data for a target store.

options.text: Extract, transform, and load
Encrypt, transfer, and log
Evaluate, train, and learn
Execute, test, and launch

summary: ETL stands for extract, transform, and load.
In RAG, document content is prepared and loaded into a searchable store.

questions.questionText: Why split long documents into chunks for RAG?
questions.hint: Smaller pieces are easier to search and pass as relevant context.

options.text: Chunks are easier to store and retrieve than treating a whole long document as one unit
Chunking guarantees that all document facts are correct
Chunks prevent the need for embeddings
Chunking automatically grants users access

summary: Chunking divides long text into smaller retrievable pieces.
Relevant chunks can be supplied as context without using an entire document.

questions.questionText: What is an embedding?
questions.hint: It represents text numerically so its meaning can be compared.

options.text: A numerical vector representation intended to capture aspects of text meaning
A human-readable API password
A JSON-RPC response identifier
A server deployment region

summary: An embedding represents text as a numerical vector.
These vectors can be compared to find semantically related text.

questions.questionText: Why is a vector database useful for RAG?
questions.hint: It can compare a query vector with stored document vectors.

options.text: It can find vectors similar to a query, supporting semantic search
It guarantees that every source is authoritative
It replaces all document preparation
It stores OAuth passwords in plain text

summary: Vector databases support similarity search over embeddings.
This can retrieve semantically relevant text even when it does not share exact keywords.

questions.questionText: What happens during retrieval after a user asks a question?
questions.hint: Relevant chunks are found and supplied as context.

options.text: The query is used to find relevant document chunks, which are returned as model context
The user's question is automatically added to model training
Every stored document is sent to the user
The vector database changes the OAuth scopes

summary: Retrieval searches for document chunks relevant to the query.
Those chunks can be included as context for generation.

questions.questionText: How can agentic RAG differ from a fixed RAG workflow?
questions.hint: The agent can decide how and when to use retrieval tools.

options.text: An agent can choose retrieval tools, inspect results, and decide whether more information is needed
It never retrieves documents
It requires every document to be placed in the model's training data
It makes the vector database responsible for generating all answers

summary: An agent can decide when to retrieve and how to use returned results.
It may make additional tool calls before giving an answer.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a document-ingestion tool in the RAG project?
questions.hint: It prepares and loads documents so they can be searched later.

options.text: Extracting and loading documents into a vector collection for later search
Granting OAuth permission to every user
Returning a final answer without retrieving data
Hosting an MCP client on a user's computer

summary: Ingestion prepares documents and adds them to the searchable collection.
Later query tools can retrieve relevant content from that collection.

questions.questionText: Why should a reload or ingestion operation avoid unintentionally duplicating old entries?
questions.hint: Running ingestion repeatedly may add the same source more than once.

options.text: Repeated ingestion may add duplicate documents, so the collection may need a controlled reset or deduplication
Duplicate entries are required for OAuth
Vector databases cannot store more than one document
The MCP client cannot read a collection with one entry

summary: Repeated ingestion can duplicate stored content if not handled carefully.
A controlled reset or deduplication strategy can help avoid duplicate entries.

questions.questionText: What does the document-query tool return to the agent?
questions.hint: The agent needs the matching content and its source context.

options.text: Relevant document results with content and source information
The server's secret environment variables
Only the user's OAuth password
A list of unrelated API endpoints

summary: The query tool returns relevant document results and source details.
A search response may also include similarity distance or a configurable result count.

questions.questionText: What is the database-status tool for?
questions.hint: It helps check whether documents have been loaded.

options.text: Reporting collection information such as the number of stored documents
Generating API keys for all clients
Replacing the document-ingestion process
Changing the MCP transport

summary: A status tool can report collection details such as its document count.
This helps developers verify whether ingestion has occurred.

questions.questionText: Why test RAG functions in a notebook before integrating them into an MCP server?
questions.hint: Test the core functions before adding the server integration layer.

options.text: It makes the underlying functions easier to develop and debug before exposing them as tools
A notebook automatically makes the tools secure for production
MCP servers cannot call Python functions
Testing first removes the need to inspect tool results

summary: Testing the underlying RAG functions separately helps isolate development and debugging.
They can then be exposed through MCP tools.
